## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

The *Zhōuyì* 周易 ("Changes of Zhōu"), conventionally rendered *Yì jīng* 易經 ("Classic of Changes") once it acquired canonical status, is the root divinatory and cosmological classic of the Confucian canon and the parent text on which the entire KR1a section comments. The Kanripo recension carried under this id is the bare received text — sixty-four hexagrams (*guà* 卦) with their hexagram statements (*guàcí* 卦辭) and line statements (*yáocí* 爻辭), followed by the ten so-called *yìzhuàn* 易傳 / *Shíyì* 十翼 ("Ten Wings"): *Tuàn* 彖 (upper and lower), *Xiàng* 象 (upper and lower), *Wényán* 文言, *Xìcí* 繫辭 (upper and lower), *Shuōguà* 說卦, *Xùguà* 序卦, and *Záguà* 雜卦. The base edition shipped here is the TLS digital text (Kanripo PROPERTY: BASEEDITION tls), without commentary.

Because the work is a layered composite (a Zhōu-period divinatory core overlaid with Warring-States to Hàn-period philosophical commentaries that were eventually canonized as part of the same "Classic"), the frontmatter dating window 900–100 BCE represents the composition-and-stabilization span of the received text as a whole, not the date of any single stratum.

**Abstract**

The *Zhōuyì* is universally agreed to be a stratified text. The *guàcí* and *yáocí* — terse, often divinatory phrases attached to hexagrams and individual lines — belong to the late Western Zhōu (conventionally ca. 9th c. BCE), as argued on linguistic, prosopographic, and ritual-context grounds by Edward L. Shaughnessy on the basis of references to specific Western Zhōu kings, marriage practices, military campaigns, and hexagram-statement formulae shared with Western Zhōu bronze inscriptions. Traditional attribution credits the trigrams to [伏羲](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BC%8F%E7%BE%B2) Fú Xī, the doubling into hexagrams and the *guàcí* to [周文王](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%91%A8%E6%96%87%E7%8E%8B) King Wén of Zhōu, and the *yáocí* to the Duke of Zhōu ([周公](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%91%A8%E5%85%AC) Zhōu Gōng); none of these attributions is sustainable on internal evidence, but they are the reason the work bears the dynastic name Zhōu.

The Ten Wings (*Shíyì*) are a heterogeneous body of philosophical and cosmological commentary appended later. Linguistic and conceptual analysis dates them broadly to the Warring States and early Hàn (4th–2nd c. BCE), with the *Xìcí* (*Dàzhuàn* 大傳) and *Shuōguà* showing the strongest cosmological-correlative thinking. The traditional ascription of the Wings to Confucius is rejected by virtually all modern scholarship; the *Lúnyǔ* 論語 nowhere quotes them, and the language is typically post-Confucian. Manuscript finds — most importantly the Mǎwángduī 馬王堆 silk *Zhōuyì* (168 BCE tomb), and the Shanghai Museum and Fùyáng 阜陽 bamboo manuscripts — confirm that by the early Western Hàn the *guà*-and-*yáo* corpus already circulated in close to its received order, while the Wings were still individually packaged (the Mǎwángduī version places its commentary chapters separately, in different order, and includes texts such as *Èrsānzǐ wèn* 二三子問 not preserved in the received recension).

The text became canonical in the early Western Hàn through the transmission line associated with [田何](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%94%B0%E4%BD%95) Tián Hé of Zīchuān 菑川, recorded in the *Hànshū Rúlín zhuàn* 漢書·儒林傳, and was established as one of the Five Classics under [漢武帝](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E6%BC%A2%E6%AD%A6%E5%B8%9D) Hàn Wǔdì (r. 141–87 BCE). Its received form has been textually stable since the [王弼](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E5%BC%BC) Wáng Bì (226–249, [KR1a0006](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR1/KR1a/KR1a0006)) recension supplanted the Hàn *xiàngshù* 象數 schools in the early medieval period. The standard Sòng-imperial print line runs through [孔穎達](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AD%94%E7%A9%8E%E9%81%94) Kǒng Yǐngdá's *Zhōuyì zhèngyì* 周易正義 ([KR1a0007](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR1/KR1a/KR1a0007)), and the Sìkù 四庫 version of the canonical text is the one transmitted in the *Shísān jīng zhùshū* 十三經注疏.

The core hermeneutic divisions in the later commentarial tradition — between the *xiàngshù* 象數 ("image-and-number") school descending from Hàn-Yì masters such as [孟喜](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%AD%9F%E5%96%9C) Mèng Xǐ, [京房](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E4%BA%AC%E6%88%BF) Jīng Fáng, [鄭玄](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E9%84%AD%E7%8E%84) Zhèng Xuán ([KR1a0003](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR1/KR1a/KR1a0003), [KR1a0004](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR1/KR1a/KR1a0004)), and [虞翻](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E8%99%9E%E7%BF%BB) Yú Fān, and the *yìlǐ* 義理 ("meaning-and-pattern") school descending from Wáng Bì — structure the entire KR1a corpus that follows.
